claim: The D.N.J. court denied Apple's motion to dismiss the DOJ's Section 2 monopolization suit on June 30, 2025, finding DOJ sufficiently pled Apple monopoly power in US smartphone and performance-smartphone markets.
scope_conditions: US District Court for D.N.J., case 2:24-cv-04055, pleading stage only
quoted_support: On June 30, 2025, the US District Court for the District of New Jersey denied Apple's Motion to Dismiss the U.S. Department of Justice's lawsuit accusing the company of violating Section 2 of the Sherman Antitrust Act.

claim: The court found Apple's alleged US market shares of 65% (smartphones) and 70% (performance smartphones) sufficient to allege monopoly power, rejecting Apple's global-market defense.
quoted_support: the court determined Apple's alleged US market shares within the government's asserted markets (65% for smartphones and 70% for performance smartphones) are high enough to allege monopoly power.

claim: The court rejected Apple's refusal-to-deal defense by analogy to the DOJ v. Google ad-tech ruling, holding that restrictions on developers/users (not failure to deal with rivals) fall outside that doctrine.
scope_conditions: D.N.J. pleading-stage ruling citing E.D. Va. April 2025 Google ad-tech decision
quoted_support: Plaintiffs do not allege Apple is failing to deal with its smartphone rivals, but rather that Apple's conduct is imposing restrictions on developers and smartphone users. Courts across the country have refused to extend the refusal to deal doctrine to such conduct.

claim: Surviving DOJ allegations include Apple prohibiting developers from accessing NFC hardware necessary for cross-platform tap-to-pay digital wallets, directly implicating Apple Pay's protected market position.
stance_target: regulatory threat to Apple Pay exclusivity
scope_conditions: allegations surviving motion to dismiss, not proven at trial
quoted_support: Such conduct includes...prohibiting developers from accessing necessary hardware to incorporate tap-to-pay in cross-platform digital wallets.

claim: Mintz characterizes the DOJ case as likely a 'years-long battle' given Apple's vigorous defense and the case proceeding to discovery.
quoted_support: We expect Apple to vigorously defend the suit in what could become a years-long battle.
